newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire jungle reveals more human misery.
newsitem.headline: Zaire jungle reveals more human misery.

text.p: The jungle offered up more haunting visions of human misery from Zaire's civil war, whose end still looked as likely through a rebel military victory as through peace talks.
In north Zaire, exhausted Rwandan Hutu refugees on the move since the rebels overran their camps last year collapsed and died along a railway. Journalists saw a baby die in its mother's arms.
In the south of the country, expatriate sources said the rebels, fresh from agreeing to talks with the government, had seized the small town of Kasenga on the Zambian border.
The capture, which would bring them within a 10-hour truck drive of Zaire's second city Lubumbashi in the southern copper belt, was denied by defence ministry officials.
Reports of Kasenga's fall came the morning after Laurent Kabila's rebels and the crumbling government of President Mobutu Sese Seko agreed to meet for their first peace talks.
The agreement, reached at an African summit in Togo, was immediately fraught with trouble.
The rebels reject a truce before talks, which they say must discuss not whether the ailing 66-year-old Mobutu transfers power, but how and when.
"Rebel strategy centres around talking while fighting and fighting while talking," a regional military source said.
Rebels said the talks would start on Easter Monday or a day later and a government source in South Africa confirmed a meeting there was on the cards.
But in Kinshasa, Mobutu's spokesman rejected the rebel agenda and denied a firm date for talks had yet been agreed.

In and around Ubilo, a village 82 km (50 miles) south of rebel-held Kisangani in northeastern Zaire, aid workers and journalists saw the appalling plight of about 75,000 of the Rwandan Hutu refugees trapped in the war zone.
At least 500 have been buried since March 16 at Ubilo, according to Lubinga Nganda, head of a Zairean Red Cross team.
More than a million Hutus fled camps on the Rwandan and Burundian border last October and November at the start of a campaign by rebels fighting the Zairean army.
Around 600,000 returned to Rwanda in November but hundreds of thousands more, some armed, fled west into the jungle.
Emaciated refugees, some almost skeletal, were attempting to walk towards aid at Kisangani but those too weak to start the trek lay dead and dying within the abandoned Ubilo camp.
Some huddled by a railway were dying of malaria, dysentery, fatigue and malnutrition, a Zaire Red Cross nurse said.
"There has been a selection. The fittest make it but the unfit die," said Kilian Kleinschmidt, a U.N. emergency officer.
